mainEntity.name: How many keywords are there in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java has 67 reserved keywords as of Java 21 (2026). This includes 51 traditional keywords (like class, public, static, etc.), 16 contextual/restricted keywords added in modern Java (like var, record, sealed, permits, yield). The keywords 'goto' and 'const' are reserved but unused. 'true', 'false', and 'null' are literals, not keywords — a common interview trap.

mainEntity.name: Can we use Java keywords as variable names?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Java keywords are reserved words and cannot be used as identifiers (variable names, class names, method names). Attempting to do so causes a compile-time error. For example: 'int class = 5;' is illegal. However, contextual keywords like 'var', 'record', and 'sealed' have limited reserved scope — they cannot be used as type names in their respective contexts but may be valid as variable names in older codebases.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: These are three completely different concepts: 'final' is a keyword used to make variables constant, prevent method overriding, or prevent class inheritance. 'finally' is a keyword used in try-catch blocks — the finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception occurred. 'finalize()' is a deprecated method of the Object class that was called by the GC before destroying an object — removed/deprecated since Java 9.

mainEntity.name: What does the 'var' keyword do in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Introduced in Java 10, 'var' enables local variable type inference. Instead of writing 'ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>()', you write 'var list = new ArrayList<String>()'. The compiler infers the type from the right-hand side expression. Importantly, var is still strongly typed — once inferred, the type cannot change. It is NOT dynamic typing like Python. var can only be used for local variables, not for fields, method parameters, or return types.

mainEntity.name: What are sealed classes in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Introduced in Java 17 (finalized), sealed classes let you restrict which classes can extend or implement them, using the 'sealed' keyword with a 'permits' clause. Example: 'public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle'. This gives the developer total control over the class hierarchy — unlike abstract classes which allow any class to extend them. Sealed classes pair perfectly with pattern matching and switch expressions in modern Java.

blocks.text: Java keywords (also called reserved words) are predefined, case-sensitive tokens that have a fixed, specific meaning in the Java language syntax. They are part of the Java Language Specification (JLS) and cannot be used as identifiers — meaning you cannot name your variables, classes, methods, or packages using a keyword.

As of Java 21 LTS (2026), Java has 67 reserved keywords. This includes traditional keywords like class, public, static, and newer additions like var, record, sealed, and permits. Two keywords — goto and const — are reserved but not used in Java, inherited from C/C++ to prevent confusion.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Classic Interview Trap
blocks.text: "true", "false", and "null" are NOT keywords in Java — they are literals. However, they are also reserved and cannot be used as identifiers. This is a very common trick question in Java interviews.

blocks.title: 💡 Case Sensitivity Matters
blocks.text: Java keywords are strictly lowercase. Writing "Class" or "PUBLIC" does NOT create a keyword conflict — these are valid identifiers. But "class" and "public" are keywords. Java is 100% case-sensitive.

Memorizing 67 keywords alphabetically is ineffective. The smart approach is to learn them by functional category. Here's the authoritative breakdown:

blocks.text: Access modifiers are among the most critical keywords in Java. They enforce encapsulation — one of the four pillars of OOP — by controlling which parts of your codebase can access which members.
🔓 public

public is the widest access modifier. A public class, method, or field is accessible from anywhere — same class, same package, subclass in another package, or completely unrelated class in any package. Every Java application has exactly one public class whose name must match the filename.

blocks.label: PublicExample.java
lines: balance += amount; // Called from any class

blocks.text: 🔒 private

private is the strictest access modifier. A private member is accessible only within the same class. It is the backbone of encapsulation — hiding internal implementation from the outside world. Best practice: make all fields private and expose them via public getters/setters.

blocks.label: PrivateExample.java
lines: private double balance; // Hidden from outside
private String pin;     // Only accessible inside BankAccount

blocks.text: 🛡️ protected

protected access allows visibility within the same package AND all subclasses, even in different packages. It is used primarily in inheritance hierarchies to allow child classes to access parent members without making them fully public.
📦 default (package-private)

When no access modifier is specified, Java uses default (package-private) access. The member is accessible only within the same package. There is no default keyword for this — its absence IS the default.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Interview Trap: default keyword vs default access
blocks.text: The 'default' keyword in a switch statement and the default access modifier are completely different concepts. 'default' in switch provides fallback logic. Default access (no modifier) restricts access to the package. In interfaces, 'default' keyword (Java 8+) defines a concrete method. Don't confuse these three uses!

sections.title: Class & Object Keywords — OOP in Action

blocks.text: These keywords form the backbone of Java's object-oriented paradigm. Mastering them means mastering OOP itself.
🏗️ class

class is used to declare a new class — the fundamental building block of Java programs. Every piece of Java code lives inside a class. A class defines a blueprint: it declares fields (state) and methods (behavior). You instantiate a class using new to create objects.
🔗 extends vs implements

extends is used for class inheritance (a class extends another class) and interface inheritance (an interface extends another interface). implements is used when a class implements an interface. Java supports single class inheritance (extends only one class) but multiple interface implementation (implements many interfaces).

blocks.label: InheritanceExample.java
lines: class Duck extends Animal implements Flyable, Swimmable {

blocks.text: 📌 this

this refers to the current object instance. It has four primary uses: (1) Disambiguate instance variables from local variables when names clash. (2) Call another constructor in the same class — this(...). (3) Pass the current object as a method argument. (4) Return the current object from a method (used in builder patterns).

blocks.label: ThisKeyword.java
lines: public Employee(String name, int age, String department) {
this.name = name;           // Disambiguate field vs param

blocks.text: 🧬 super

super refers to the immediate parent class. It has three uses: (1) Access parent class fields hidden by child class fields. (2) Call parent class methods overridden by child. (3) Call parent class constructor — super(...) must be the first statement in the child constructor.
🆕 new

new allocates memory on the heap and creates a new object instance of a class. It calls the class constructor to initialize the object. Without new, you have only a reference variable pointing to null.
🔍 instanceof

instanceof tests whether an object is an instance of a specific class or implements an interface. Returns true or false. Java 16+ introduced Pattern Matching for instanceof — eliminating the ugly cast that follows.

blocks.label: InstanceofPatternMatching.java
lines: String s = (String) obj; // Manual cast needed

The switch statement has undergone massive evolution. Java 14+ introduced Switch Expressions with arrow syntax, eliminating fall-through bugs and verbose break statements. Java 21 adds pattern matching support — making switch one of the most powerful constructs in modern Java.

blocks.text: 🔁 Labeled break and continue

Most developers know break and continue. Fewer know their labeled forms — which allow breaking or continuing an outer loop from inside a nested loop. This is one of the most underused features in Java.

blocks.label: LabeledBreak.java

// Without label: inner break only exits j-loop
// With label: breaks out of both loops entirely

blocks.title: 🚨 Critical: final vs finally vs finalize()
blocks.text: This is the most common Java interview question globally. final = keyword to make variables/methods/classes immutable/non-overridable. finally = exception keyword for cleanup code that always runs. finalize() = a deprecated method of Object class (removed from use in Java 9+) — NOT a keyword. sections.title: Concurrency & Memory Keywords — synchronized and volatile

blocks.text: Java has two built-in keywords specifically for thread safety: synchronized and volatile. While the java.util.concurrent package provides higher-level tools, these keywords are the foundation that every Java developer must understand deeply.
🔒 synchronized

synchronized ensures that only one thread at a time can execute a block of code. It works by acquiring a monitor lock (intrinsic lock) on an object. Can be applied to methods or code blocks. It guarantees both mutual exclusion (atomicity) and memory visibility.

blocks.label: SynchronizedExample.java
lines: count++; // Thread-safe: only one thread at a time
count--; // Only this block is synchronized
// Static synchronized — locks on Counter.class object

blocks.text: ⚡ volatile

volatile guarantees that reads and writes to a variable go directly to main memory (not the CPU cache). This ensures visibility across threads — when one thread modifies a volatile variable, other threads immediately see the updated value. Unlike synchronized, volatile does NOT guarantee atomicity for compound operations like count++.

blocks.label: VolatileExample.java
lines: // Without volatile: thread B might read stale cached value
// With volatile: all threads always read from main memory
// Thread A calls this to stop the server
isRunning = false; // Immediately visible to Thread B
// Thread B runs this loop — needs latest value of isRunning
while (isRunning) { // Reads fresh value every iteration

rows: ✅ Yes — one thread at a time
❌ No — multiple threads can read simultaneously
❌ No — count++ is NOT atomic with volatile

blocks.text: 📦 transient

transient marks a field to be excluded from serialization. When an object is serialized (converted to a byte stream), transient fields are skipped and reset to their default values upon deserialization. Used for sensitive data (passwords, keys) or non-serializable objects.

blocks.label: TransientExample.java
lines: private String username;    // Will be serialized
private transient String password; // NEVER serialized
private transient int sessionToken; // Excluded from byte stream

blocks.text: Java has exactly 8 primitive types, each represented by a keyword. Primitives are stored on the stack (not heap), are passed by value, and have fixed sizes regardless of platform — ensuring portability.

blocks.title: 💡 Pro Tip: Never Use float for Money
blocks.text: Never use 'float' or 'double' for financial calculations due to floating-point precision errors. 0.1 + 0.2 in double = 0.30000000000000004. Use java.math.BigDecimal for exact decimal arithmetic in banking, e-commerce, and fintech applications.

blocks.label: PrimitiveExamples.java
lines: long  l = 9_000_000_000L; // L suffix required for long literals
float f = 3.14f;          // f suffix required for float
char  c = 'A';            // Single quotes for char

sections.title: Modern Java Keywords (Java 10–21) — The Game Changers

blocks.text: Modern Java (10–21) introduced a wave of new keywords and contextual identifiers that fundamentally modernize how Java is written. These additions close the gap between Java and newer languages like Kotlin and Scala.
🔷 var — Local Variable Type Inference (Java 10)

var allows the compiler to infer the type of a local variable from its initializer. Java remains statically typed — var is resolved at compile-time, not runtime. It eliminates redundancy without sacrificing type safety.

blocks.label: VarKeyword.java
lines: // ✅ var — less redundancy, same type safety
var map  = new HashMap<String, Integer>(); // HashMap<String,Integer>
// ❌ var NOT allowed: fields, method params, return types
// var field = "hello";  // Compile error — fields can't use var
// public var getName() { return name; }  // Compile error
// ❌ var must be initialized — type can't be inferred from null
// var x = null;  // Compile error — ambiguous type

blocks.text: 📋 record — Immutable Data Classes (Java 16)

record declares an immutable data carrier class. In one line, it automatically generates: a canonical constructor, private final fields, getters (no 'get' prefix), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Replaces hundreds of lines of boilerplate DTO/POJO code.

blocks.label: RecordKeyword.java
lines: // ONE line replaces ~80 lines of traditional POJO code
public record Point(double x, double y) {}
// - double x() and double y() accessors
// Records with compact constructor — add validation
public record Person(String name, int age) {

blocks.text: 🔐 sealed + permits — Controlled Inheritance (Java 17)

sealed restricts which classes can extend or implement a type, using a permits clause. This gives you exhaustive control over your type hierarchy — a tool for building airtight domain models. Permitted subclasses must be declared as final, sealed, or non-sealed.

blocks.label: SealedClasses.java
lines: // Sealed class: ONLY Circle, Rectangle, Triangle can extend Shape
public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
public final class Circle extends Shape {       // final: no further extension
public sealed class Rectangle extends Shape    // sealed: further restricted
public non-sealed class Triangle extends Shape {} // open to extension
// The payoff: exhaustive pattern matching in switch
case Circle    c -> Math.PI * c.radius * c.radius;
// No 'default' needed! Compiler knows all cases are covered.

blocks.text: ⚡ yield — Switch Expression Return (Java 14)
yield returns a value from a switch expression block. It is the equivalent of return inside a switch block — when you need multi-statement logic in a case branch but also need to produce a value.
Certain Java keywords cause consistent confusion — even for experienced developers. Here are the most common traps with expert-level explanations.

items.title: static — The Shared State Trap
items.text: static means a field or method belongs to the CLASS, not any instance. static fields are shared across ALL objects. Mutating a static field from one instance affects all others — a common source of bugs in multithreaded applications. Never make mutable shared state static without synchronization.

items.title: final — Three Different Meanings
items.text: final on a variable = constant (cannot reassign the reference). final on a method = cannot be overridden. final on a class = cannot be extended (e.g., String is final). Note: final on an object reference only prevents reassignment — the object's internal state can still be mutated.

items.title: abstract — Can't Be Instantiated
items.text: abstract on a class = cannot create objects directly, must be subclassed. abstract on a method = no body defined, subclass MUST implement. An abstract class CAN have concrete methods, fields, constructors. A class with even ONE abstract method must be declared abstract.

items.title: return in finally — Silent Killer
items.text: If you put a return statement inside a finally block, it SUPPRESSES any exception being propagated and overrides any return value from the try block. This is one of the worst Java anti-patterns. Never use return inside a finally block.

items.title: synchronized ≠ volatile
items.text: synchronized ensures atomicity AND visibility. volatile ensures only visibility. Using volatile for compound operations like i++ is incorrect — i++ is not atomic (it's read-modify-write: three operations). Use synchronized, AtomicInteger, or java.util.concurrent.locks for compound operations.

items.title: goto & const — Reserved but Forbidden
items.text: Java reserved 'goto' and 'const' from C/C++ but intentionally left them unused. This prevents programmers who know C/C++ from accidentally using them. Using goto or const causes a compile error in Java — they exist only to block their use as identifiers.

blocks.label: FinalPitfall.java
lines: list.add("Python"); // ✅ Valid — list is NOT immutable
// list = new ArrayList<>(); // ❌ Compile error — can't reassign
// To make truly immutable: use List.of() or Collections.unmodifiableList()

sections.title: Java Keywords — Interview Questions (Beginner to Advanced)

blocks.text: These are the highest-frequency Java keyword interview questions across product companies, service companies, and startups. Mastering these answers will set you apart.

items.q: Q1. How many keywords are there in Java and can you name the unused ones?
items.a: Java has 67 reserved keywords as of Java 21 (2026), including traditional keywords and modern contextual keywords (var, record, sealed, permits, yield, when). Two keywords are reserved but UNUSED in Java: 'goto' and 'const' — inherited from C/C++ but intentionally non-functional. They cannot be used as identifiers but also have no syntax. Also note: 'true', 'false', 'null' are literals, NOT keywords.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between static and instance methods?
items.a: A static method belongs to the class — it can be called as ClassName.method() without creating any object. It cannot access instance fields (non-static) or use 'this'. An instance method belongs to an object — it is called on an instance (obj.method()) and can access both static and instance members. The main() method is static so the JVM can call it before any objects are created.

items.q: Q3. Can a constructor be static? final? abstract?
items.a: No to all three. A static constructor is meaningless — constructors are called on instances via 'new', not on classes. A final constructor makes no sense — constructors are not inherited so there's nothing to prevent overriding. An abstract constructor is impossible — abstract requires an incomplete method body, but constructors must always be fully defined for instantiation to work. The compiler rejects all three.

items.q: Q4. Explain the difference between throw and throws with code.
items.a: 'throw' is used INSIDE a method body to actually throw an exception object: throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative age"). 'throws' is used in the METHOD SIGNATURE to declare that this method might propagate checked exceptions to its caller: public void readFile() throws IOException. throw is a statement. throws is a clause. throw requires an exception object. throws requires exception class names.

items.q: Q5. What is the significance of the 'strictfp' keyword?
items.a: 'strictfp' (strict floating point) was introduced in Java 1.2 to ensure consistent floating-point calculations across all hardware architectures. When applied to a class or method, it forces all float/double calculations to follow IEEE 754 standard strictly — preventing processors from using extended precision registers. As of Java 17, the JVM mandates strict floating-point semantics globally, making strictfp effectively redundant (though still legal syntax).

items.q: Q6. What does 'native' keyword mean in Java?
items.a: 'native' declares a method whose implementation is written in a platform-specific language (typically C or C++) rather than Java. The Java Native Interface (JNI) bridges Java code and native libraries. Example: System.currentTimeMillis() is declared native because it calls OS-level timing functions. Native methods have no body in Java: just 'private native int nativeMethod();'. They are compiled into .dll (Windows) or .so (Linux) files.

items.q: Q7. Can we use 'var' as a variable name in Java 10+?
items.a: Yes! Despite being a contextual keyword for type inference, 'var' can still be used as a variable name, method name, or package name for backward compatibility. Only its use as a TYPE NAME is restricted. So: 'var var = 5;' actually compiles — the first 'var' is the type inference keyword, and the second 'var' is the variable name. This is strange but valid. It's strongly discouraged in new code.

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between 'break' and 'return' inside a finally block?
items.a: 'return' inside a finally block suppresses any exception being propagated and overrides any return value from the try or catch block — making it one of the worst Java anti-patterns. 'break' inside finally (within a loop) exits the loop but doesn't suppress exceptions. Both should be avoided in finally blocks. finally should only contain cleanup code (closing resources), never control flow statements.

items.q: Q9. What are sealed classes and when should you use them?
items.a: Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes can extend them via a 'permits' clause. Use them when you have a closed, well-defined type hierarchy where you want exhaustive control — like an algebraic data type in functional languages. They pair perfectly with pattern matching in switch expressions, allowing the compiler to verify that all cases are handled without a default clause. Ideal for: Result types (Success/Failure), State machines, Expression trees, Domain events.

items.q: Q10. What is the 'assert' keyword and why is it disabled by default?
items.a: 'assert' enables runtime assertions for debugging — it throws AssertionError if a condition is false: assert x > 0 : 'x must be positive'. Assertions are DISABLED by default at runtime. You must enable them with the JVM flag: java -ea MyApp. They are disabled by default because: (1) they affect performance, (2) production code should use proper exceptions, not assertions. Use assert for development/testing invariants, never for production validation.

items.q: 3. What happens if a try block has a return statement AND a finally block? Which executes first?
items.a: The finally block ALWAYS executes, even when the try block has a return statement. Java evaluates the return value in try, then executes finally, then returns. If finally also has a return statement, it overrides the try's return value — a silent bug. Order: try return value evaluated → finally executes → if finally has return, it wins; otherwise try's value is returned.

items.q: 4. Can an abstract class have a constructor? If yes, when is it called?
items.a: Yes! Abstract classes CAN and SHOULD have constructors, even though you can't instantiate them directly. The abstract class constructor is called when a concrete subclass is instantiated via super(). It's used to initialize fields defined in the abstract class. The JVM always calls the parent constructor chain — abstract or not.

items.a: abstract and static cannot be combined. abstract means the method has no body and MUST be overridden by a subclass (requires object polymorphism). static means the method belongs to the class and is resolved at compile time (bypasses polymorphism). These two concepts are fundamentally contradictory — static methods cannot participate in runtime polymorphism, so they cannot be abstract.

items.q: 8. In a switch expression using '->' arrows, when do you need 'yield'?
items.a: yield is only needed inside a block ({}) in a switch expression when you need multi-statement logic before returning a value. Arrow cases with a single expression don't need yield — the expression IS the value. Example requiring yield: case COMPLEX -> { log(); compute(); yield result; }. Simple case not needing it: case SIMPLE -> computeValue();

blocks.text: Java keywords are not just syntax — they are the building blocks of every program you will ever write. Each keyword encodes a design decision made by the Java Language Designers: decisions about safety (final, private), performance (volatile, synchronized), expressiveness (record, var, sealed), and portability (the entire JVM model).

The evolution from Java 1.0's original keywords to Java 21's record, sealed, and when tells the story of a language that refuses to stagnate. Modern Java keywords close the expressiveness gap with Kotlin and Scala while maintaining the reliability and ecosystem that enterprise teams depend on.
